subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 58-year-old man presents with a hoarse voice and a new blowing, high-pitched early diastolic murmur heard along the left sternal border. His pupils accommodate but do not react to light. A fluorescent treponemal antibody test is positive. Imaging shows marked dilation of the aortic root and ascending aorta.
question: Which of the following mechanisms is most likely responsible for the aortic dilation in this patient?

options.text: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
Transmural inflammation of all three aortic layers with extracellular matrix degradation
Cholesterol microembolization into the vasa vasorum
Intimal tear creating a false lumen within the aortic wall
Concentric smooth muscle proliferation ('onion skinning') of the aortic vasa vasorum

explanation_correct: Thoracic aortic aneurysm is associated with tertiary (3°) syphilis, which damages the aortic vasa vasorum by obliterative endarteritis, starving the aortic wall and causing aneurysmal dilation of the root and ascending aorta. The Argyll Robertson pupils (accommodate but do not react to light) confirm neurosyphilis. Root dilation stretches the aortic valve annulus, producing aortic regurgitation, which explains the early diastolic murmur.

explanation_incorrect.B: Transmural inflammation with extracellular matrix degradation is the mechanism of abdominal aortic aneurysm, not the syphilitic thoracic aneurysm.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cholesterol microembolization affects small distal arteries after vascular procedures and does not cause aortic wall destruction or root aneurysm.
explanation_incorrect.D: An intimal tear with false lumen describes aortic dissection, which is a distinct entity from the aneurysmal dilation seen here.
explanation_incorrect.E: 'Onion skinning' describes hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis of severe hypertension in small arterioles, not syphilitic aortitis.

educationalObjective: Link tertiary syphilis to thoracic aortic aneurysm via obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, with aortic root dilation causing aortic regurgitation.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 74-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at home. He is in severe distress with abdominal and back pain. His blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg and does not improve despite rapid intravenous fluids. Examination reveals a tender, pulsatile mass in the mid-abdomen.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Acute pancreatitis
Aortic dissection involving the ascending aorta
Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
Perforated peptic ulcer with sepsis
Acute mesenteric ischemia

explanation_correct: Rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm classically presents as the triad of a pulsatile abdominal mass, acute abdominal/back pain, and hypotension that is resistant to fluid resuscitation. A pulsatile mass with shock makes this diagnosis and requires emergent surgical management. Localized pathologic dilation of the aorta may cause abdominal and/or back pain as a sign of leaking, dissection, or imminent rupture.

explanation_incorrect.A: Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back but does not produce a pulsatile abdominal mass.
explanation_incorrect.B: Ascending aortic dissection presents with tearing chest pain radiating to the back and possible pulse deficits or aortic regurgitation, not a pulsatile abdominal mass with hypotension.
explanation_incorrect.D: A perforated ulcer causes peritonitis with a rigid, non-pulsatile abdomen rather than a pulsatile mass.
explanation_incorrect.E: Mesenteric ischemia presents with severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings and no abdominal mass.

educationalObjective: Recognize the rupture triad of abdominal aortic aneurysm: pulsatile abdominal mass, acute abdominal/back pain, and resistant hypotension.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: An 80-year-old man dies after a ruptured aneurysm. Autopsy reveals an aneurysm of the abdominal aorta located entirely distal to the renal arteries, with transmural inflammation and extracellular matrix degradation of the wall. The aorta above the renal arteries appears relatively normal.
question: Which of the following best explains the typical location of this patient's aneurysm?

options.text: Higher transluminal pressure in the infrarenal segment than in the juxtarenal aorta
The distribution of vasa vasorum is reduced in the infrarenal aorta
Turbulent flow at the aortic bifurcation injures the wall below the renal arteries
Atherosclerotic plaques preferentially spare the infrarenal segment
The infrarenal aorta has a thicker media and greater elastic content

explanation_correct: Abdominal aortic aneurysm is most often infrarenal because the distribution of vasa vasorum is reduced in the infrarenal aorta, leaving that segment more vulnerable to transmural inflammation and extracellular matrix degradation. Risk factors include tobacco smoking (the strongest risk factor), increased age, male sex, and family history.

explanation_incorrect.A: Luminal pressure is essentially the same throughout the abdominal aorta; location is explained by the vasa vasorum supply, not a pressure gradient.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bifurcation turbulence is not the accepted explanation in the source material; the aneurysm typically arises in the infrarenal aorta because of its reduced vasa vasorum distribution.
explanation_incorrect.D: Atherosclerosis is in fact prominent in the infrarenal aorta; plaques do not spare this segment.
explanation_incorrect.E: A thicker, more elastic infrarenal media would resist dilation; it does not explain the aneurysm's typical infrarenal location.

educationalObjective: Recall that abdominal aortic aneurysms are most often infrarenal because the vasa vasorum distribution is reduced there.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 22-year-old tall, slender man whose arm span exceeds his height is evaluated for a murmur. He has superior displacement of the crystalline lens of both eyes and mitral valve prolapse. Imaging shows dilation of the aortic root. His maternal uncle died of a ruptured aortic aneurysm.
question: Which of the following underlies thoracic aortic aneurysm formation in this patient?

options.text: Transmural inflammation of all three layers of the aorta
Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
Hyaline thickening of the aortic vasa vasorum
Cystic medial degeneration
Fibrinoid necrosis of the aortic media

explanation_correct: Thoracic aortic aneurysm is associated with cystic medial degeneration, and risk factors include hypertension, bicuspid aortic valve, and connective tissue diseases such as Marfan syndrome. This patient's tall stature, arm span exceeding height, lens dislocation, and mitral valve prolapse identify Marfan syndrome, and root dilation can lead to aortic regurgitation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Transmural inflammation with extracellular matrix degradation characterizes abdominal aortic aneurysm, not the thoracic aneurysm of Marfan syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.B: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the mechanism of the thoracic aneurysm associated with tertiary syphilis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis affects small arterioles in hypertension and diabetes, not the proximal aorta.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles is seen in hypertensive emergency, not in Marfan-associated thoracic aneurysm.

educationalObjective: Associate thoracic aortic aneurysm with cystic medial degeneration, seen in Marfan syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve, and hypertension.
